what: PTC Therapeutics develops and sells medicines for rare genetic disorders. Its marketed products include Translarna and Emflaza for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Evrysdi royalties for spinal muscular atrophy (partnered with Roche), and Sephience for the metabolic disorder PKU, approved in 2025.
customers: Specialists treating rare diseases, their patients, and governments and insurers that pay for the drugs; also partners such as Roche and Novartis that pay royalties and milestones.
money: Emflaza, Translarna, Sephience and other rare-disease drugs sold directly.
Royalties on Roche’s Evrysdi, plus upfront and milestone payments from partners.
moat: Expertise in small-molecule drugs that change how genes are read, a commercial organisation set up for rare diseases worldwide, and royalty streams that do not depend on its own sales force.
risks: 2025’s $683M profit came mostly from a large upfront payment from Novartis for its Huntington’s disease drug. It will not repeat; the last twelve months show a $106M loss and almost no free cash flow.
Shareholders’ equity is negative ($-191M), a legacy of years of losses and royalty sales.
Translarna has struggled with regulators in Europe and the US, and Emflaza faces generic competition.
Much of the value depends on drugs still in trials or just launched, such as Sephience and votoplam for Huntington’s.
opportunities: Cash of $2.1B against $633M of debt gives several years of runway without raising money.
Sephience opens a large market: PKU is one of the more common rare diseases, and current treatments work poorly for many patients.
If the Huntington’s drug succeeds, Novartis carries the cost and PTC collects milestones and royalties.
Fifteen analysts average a target of about $100, 78% above the price, which shows how much depends on the pipeline.
watch: Sephience sales each quarter, and the next readouts for the Huntington’s programme.
view: Two numbers on PTC’s page will mislead you. The 2025 profit of $683 million was a one-time upfront payment from Novartis, not a turn to profitability; the last twelve months, which exclude most of it, show a $106 million loss and break-even cash flow. And the negative book value comes from years of losses and selling future royalties, so price-to-book means nothing here.

What you are actually buying is $2.1 billion of cash, a set of rare-disease drugs that cover their own costs but are not growing much, and two options: Sephience in PKU, already approved, and the Huntington’s programme, now funded by Novartis. At a $4.7 billion market value, net cash of about $1.5 billion means the market values the drugs and pipeline at roughly $3.2 billion.

This turns on Sephience. PKU is a large market by rare-disease standards, and if the launch reaches the sales analysts hope for, that $3 billion is too little. If it disappoints, the remaining business is worth less than today’s price. I would treat it as a pipeline bet with an unusually good cash cushion, and size it as you would any biotech: something that can halve or double on a few data points.
bull: Sephience becomes a large product and the Huntington’s drug works, and the cash pile funds it all without dilution.
bear: Sephience sells slowly, older products fade and the 2025 profit proves to have been a one-off peak.
